cards.hook: Recall it: what does rolling a loser for a credit really do?
cards.body: Before the answer: that credit came from somewhere. The market does not pay you to fix mistakes, so what did you sell to get it? Here it is: you closed the losing trade at a loss and opened a new, larger one, and the credit exists only because you added duration, size, or a closer strike. **A roll is re-entry at worse odds, not repair.** The test survives a second telling: if you would not open the new position fresh today, with no loss attached to it, you have no business rolling into it.
cards.depth: Why this one recurs: your broker displays the roll as one continuing position, which quietly converts a realized loss into an unrealized one. That accounting illusion is the whole seduction. Book the loss mentally at the moment you roll, and the decision gets honest again.

cards.hook: Backtest today's index members and you've excluded the corpses.
cards.body: Build your universe from current S&P 500 membership and you are testing on companies certified, in hindsight, as survivors. The index swaps out roughly 20 to 25 constituents a year, so over a 20-year backtest hundreds of delisted, acquired, and bankrupt names simply vanish from your sample. Any strategy that buys weakness looks brilliant, because the stocks that fell and never got up are not there to hurt it. **The dead are missing from your data.** The fix is point-in-time constituent lists: test each date against the membership that existed on that date, corpses included.
cards.depth: Survivorship bias flatters mean-reversion and value strategies most, since those deliberately hold losers. The mutual-fund literature found the same thing one level up: databases that quietly dropped dead funds overstated average returns by enough to change conclusions. If your data vendor cannot answer 'as of when,' assume the bias is in.

cards.hook: The studios finally sued an AI company, and skipped training entirely.
cards.body: In June 2025 Disney and Universal filed the first major-studio copyright suit against a generative AI company, targeting Midjourney. Notice what the complaint does not lead with: training data. The theory is output-side - the tool serves up recognizable Darth Vader, Minions, and Shrek on demand, a 'virtual vending machine' of infringing copies, in the complaint's phrase. That routes around the ingestion fair-use fight, where AI defendants had been landing wins, and into **character infringement, doctrine studios have been winning on for decades.** An output claim does not care how the model learned, only what it emits.
cards.depth: The complaint also alleges Midjourney kept generating the characters after the studios requested filters other AI firms had implemented - a willfulness record built before filing. Drafting note: AI reps and indemnities keyed only to training-data provenance miss this entire vector. Output is its own exposure and needs its own language.

cards.hook: Two underwriters, same file. Their quotes differed by half.
cards.body: Bias is the average error; noise is the scatter. In a noise audit Kahneman and colleagues reported from a large insurer, executives guessed that two underwriters quoting the identical case would differ by about 10%. The reported median difference was roughly 55%. Nobody had noticed, because judgment noise is invisible in the wild: each case gets one judge, so the disagreement never surfaces. **You cannot see noise in a single verdict.** Settlement valuations, damages estimates, price targets - anywhere professionals produce a number from a file, assume the scatter is several times what the institution believes.
cards.depth: The cheap fixes are mechanical: collect independent estimates before anyone speaks, average them, and score the components of the judgment separately before the overall call. Averaging independent judgments cancels noise directly. It does nothing for shared bias, which is exactly why the two errors need different medicine.

cards.hook: Your last task follows you into this one.
cards.body: Sophie Leroy's research on attention residue: when you switch tasks, part of your attention stays behind with the one you left, degrading performance on the task in front of you - and the residue is worst when the prior task was unfinished. That is a working-memory tax an ADHD brain can least afford, stacked on an already expensive switch. The move is a ready-to-resume note: before switching, spend 30 seconds writing exactly where you stopped and the literal next action. **Park the open loop in writing, not in your head.** Leroy's follow-up work found this brief ritual reduces residue and speeds re-engagement.
cards.depth: Mechanism, not vibes: unfinished goals stay active and keep intruding (the old Zeigarnik findings point the same direction). The written note externalizes the open loop - the same principle as keeping the to-do list outside your head. Working memory is for processing, not for holding state across an interruption.

cards.hook: Friday's option prices have already spent the weekend.
cards.body: Option models spread theta smoothly across calendar days, but market makers do not wait around for days with no trading. Into Friday's close they mark implied vol down, pre-collecting the two dead days, then mark it back up Monday morning. So a Friday short sale that looks like it harvests three days of decay is mostly buying a vol level that already reflects them. **The weekend's decay is sold in advance.** The clean way to see it: realized variance happens on trading days, and the market prices variance, not calendar time. Weekend theta is real only in the model.
cards.depth: The same markdown appears around holidays, and in reverse around scheduled events: earnings and CPI days carry extra implied variance while dead days carry almost none. Desks that quote in business time rather than calendar time avoid the illusion entirely. If your backtest credits full calendar theta over weekends, it is overstating short-premium returns.

cards.hook: Run a hundred backtests, and the best one lies.
cards.body: Suppose every strategy you test is pure noise. Test one hundred, and the best in-sample Sharpe will still look excellent, because you selected it for exactly that. The maximum of many noisy estimates is biased upward, and the bias grows with the number of trials. The reported number is not the strategy's Sharpe; it is **the winner of a tournament you ran against randomness**. Honest practice: count every variant you tried, including the ones you abandoned, discount the winner for the size of the field, or validate it on data the selection never touched.
cards.depth: Bailey and Lopez de Prado formalized the discount as the deflated Sharpe ratio, which asks whether your best result clears the bar you would expect from N tries on noise alone. Most published backtests fail that bar, which is one reason live performance so reliably disappoints.

cards.hook: The record AI copyright settlement wasn't about training at all.
cards.body: In September 2025 Anthropic agreed to pay roughly 1.5 billion dollars, reported as the largest copyright settlement ever, to authors whose books sat in its training data. The part practitioners keep missing: the court had already ruled that training on lawfully purchased books was fair use. What survived was the claim over books downloaded from pirate libraries. Liability turned on **how the copies were acquired, not what the model learned**. The drafting lesson for anyone papering AI deals: point the warranties and diligence at data provenance, the acquisition chain, because that is where the money actually moved.
cards.depth: Reported terms ran near 3,000 dollars per work across roughly half a million titles, with the pirated copies destroyed. Compare Thomson Reuters v. Ross, where training use lost outright: the fair-use question is still unsettled circuit by circuit, but the piracy question is not, and it prices at scale.

cards.hook: Recall it: why must your to-do list live outside your head?
cards.body: Two weeks ago this feed made a claim about which cognitive function ADHD taxes hardest, and what it costs to keep a plan in your head. Name the function and the move before reading on. The function is working memory. Holding your next three steps active burns the same buffer that executing the current step requires, so the held items crowd out the doing. The move: **offload every open loop to one external surface** the instant it appears. One surface, not five apps. Capture is not tidiness; it frees the scarce resource to run the task actually in front of you.
cards.depth: Retrieval strengthens memory more than rereading does, which is why this card asks before it tells. The live test two weeks on is behavioral, not conceptual: does capture happen at the moment the thought arrives? A system consulted later but not fed in the moment protects nothing.

cards.hook: Negotiate every issue at once, never one at a time.
cards.body: Issue-by-issue bargaining quietly converts a deal into a series of zero-sum fights: each point gets contested on its own, and you spend goodwill winning things you barely value. Package bargaining changes the math. Put every open issue on the table together and you can **trade across differences in priorities**: concede what is cheap to you and expensive to them, and take the reverse. Negotiation researchers push it further with multiple equivalent simultaneous offers, presenting two or three packages you value identically. Which package the counterparty pulls toward reveals their priorities without them saying a word.
cards.depth: The equal-value part is the discipline. If the packages differ in value to you, you have just made three offers and invited cherry-picking. Built honestly, simultaneous packages also read as flexible, which the research links to better counterpart satisfaction at no cost to your own outcome.

cards.hook: In contango, time alone rolls your VIX short into profit.
cards.body: VIX futures usually sit above spot, a shape called contango. If nothing else changes, each future must still fall toward the lower cash VIX as expiry approaches. Short the future and that convergence pays you even when volatility is flat. **The roll yield, not a vol forecast, is most of the return** in a short-vol carry trade. The exposure is dangerously one-sided: the same position that quietly harvests calm-day carry takes the full blow the moment the curve flips into backwardation and spot spikes above the futures you are short.
cards.depth: This is why short-vol carry looks like free money for years and then isn't. You are paid a small, steady premium for absorbing a rare, violent tail. Any strategy whose P&L is dominated by roll yield is selling insurance, and the payout you dread is precisely the event the premium was supposedly compensating you for.

cards.hook: Copyright protects only the parts of AI art you authored.
cards.body: The US Copyright Office's 2025 guidance holds that purely AI-generated output has no human author, so it gets no protection at all. What survives is your **selectable, arrangeable human contribution**: text you wrote, the sequence you chose, edits you made by hand. In the Zarya of the Dawn comic, the Office kept the writer's story and page layout but stripped protection from the Midjourney images themselves. Prompting, however elaborate, was treated as requesting a result rather than authoring one. The generated image, on its own, belongs to no one.
cards.depth: The commercial fallout is real: an AI-heavy ad or piece of key art can be freely copied, because the machine-made pixels sit in the public domain the instant they exist. Protect the deal by contracting over the human-authored elements and by building in genuine editing passes that leave a documentable authorship trail.

cards.hook: You'd pay about the same to save 2,000 birds or 200,000.

cards.body: In a classic study, people asked what they'd pay to save migrating birds from oil ponds gave roughly the same figure whether the toll was 2,000, 20,000, or 200,000. The mind does not multiply. It answers a **prototype question instead of a quantity one**: it pictures one oil-soaked bird, prices that feeling, and ignores the count entirely. This is scope insensitivity, and it quietly wrecks any valuation driven by magnitude, from charitable giving to jury damages to how you size a vivid, low-probability tail you can easily imagine.
cards.depth: The trading version: a story about one catastrophic scenario feels equally frightening at 2% or 0.2%, so you overpay for hedges priced off vividness rather than frequency. The correction is mechanical. Force the number back in, because expected value is count times consequence, and your gut handed you only the consequence.

cards.hook: Make time take up space you can physically see.
cards.body: ADHD blunts the internal sense of time passing, so a deadline three hours out feels the same as three days out, right up until it is suddenly now. The move is to **externalize duration into something visual**: a countdown that shows remaining time as a shrinking colored wedge, not digits. Digits still make you compute how much is left, a working-memory step you keep skipping. A shrinking area is perceived directly, no computation required, so the passage of time registers as a physical event happening in front of you instead of an abstract fact you forget to check.
cards.depth: The principle scales. A wall calendar you can't avoid seeing beats a phone calendar you must decide to open. Any executive function you are weak at should be moved out of your head and into the environment, where raw perception does the monitoring your internal clock refuses to do.

cards.hook: A precise first offer anchors harder than a round one.
cards.body: Round numbers read as placeholders. Open at $10,000 and the other side hears "around ten, negotiable." Open at $9,850 and they infer you did actual math, that the figure rests on something, and they **adjust in smaller increments away from your anchor**. Research on anchor precision reports that counteroffers land closer to a precise opening and the final split tilts toward whoever set it. The precision itself signals information you may not even possess, which is why a lazy round counter so often concedes ground before a single term has actually been argued.
cards.depth: Use it on purpose. When you open, pick a defensible non-round number and be ready to explain it, because a precise anchor you can't justify invites the "where did that come from" challenge that resets the frame back to round. Precision is a claim of knowledge. Make sure the claim is real.

cards.hook: Short-dated options are gamma bets; long-dated ones are vega bets.
cards.body: Gamma and vega both scale with time to expiry, but in opposite directions. Gamma runs with the inverse square root of time, so a near-dated option whips around with spot. Vega runs with the square root of time, so a far-dated option reprices hard when implied vol shifts. **A weekly short strangle and a two-year one are different animals with the same name.** The weekly's real risk is a gap in the underlying. The LEAP's real risk is a repricing of volatility you may hold for months.
cards.depth: This is why front-month sellers obsess over pin risk and gaps, while long-dated sellers obsess over the vol surface. Same trade name, different greek doing the damage. Size and hedge to the greek that actually dominates your expiry, not the one the strategy label implies.

cards.hook: Tennessee made your voice a property right against AI.
cards.body: Tennessee's old publicity law, written in the Elvis era, protected name, photograph, and likeness. The 2024 ELVIS Act adds voice explicitly, and goes further: it targets the tools. **Liability reaches anyone who distributes software whose primary purpose is cloning a person's voice or likeness without consent.** Most publicity statutes only reach the party who commercially exploits the fake. This one reaches the maker of the generator itself. It took effect July 1, 2024, the first US law aimed squarely at generative voice cloning.
cards.depth: The practitioner miss is treating it like ordinary right-of-publicity. The toolmaker exposure is new, and it does not require the cloned person to be a celebrity or the use to be commercial in the traditional sense. Watch for other states copying the structure.

cards.hook: Your ADHD med is inert until your blood cuts it apart.
cards.body: Lisdexamfetamine is d-amphetamine chemically bonded to the amino acid lysine. Swallowed, it is pharmacologically inert. Enzymes in your red blood cells slowly cleave off the lysine, releasing active drug at a pace the enzyme controls, not your gut. **The conversion is rate-limited, so the peak stays capped and the curve stays smooth.** Practical reads: the route cannot cheat it, crushing or snorting does nothing; food barely shifts timing; and raising the dose mostly stretches the area under the curve rather than sharpening the spike.
cards.depth: This is why titration feels gradual instead of a switch flipping, and why a too-low dose reads as 'barely noticeable' rather than wrong. The design trades a fast, abusable peak for a steady one. Judge a dose over weeks at steady state, not on day three.

cards.hook: Perfect calibration can still make you a useless forecaster.
cards.body: Predict the base rate every time. Say 30 percent for every applicant when 30 percent succeed, and over enough trials you are perfectly calibrated: your 30 percent calls come true 30 percent of the time. But you have said nothing useful, because you cannot separate winners from losers. The missing quality is **resolution**, the willingness to move off the base rate when you actually know something. The Brier score splits into exactly these two parts. Superforecasters win on resolution, pushing to 5 and 95 and being right, not on calibration alone.
cards.depth: Calibration is table stakes and easy to fake by hugging the base rate. Resolution is the hard, valuable part, and it is where information actually lives. When you score your own trading or legal calls, track both, or you will reward timid forecasts that never risk being wrong.

cards.hook: Where in a long prompt does a model quietly lose your instruction?
cards.body: Think back to the U-shaped attention card. Models attend most to the very start and the very end of a context, and sag in the middle. Take a beat before the answer: the danger zone is **the middle**. Bury a load-bearing constraint halfway through a long context and it gets underweighted, even though it is technically present and retrievable. The researchers called it 'lost in the middle.' So put the task and the constraints that must hold at the top or the bottom, never in the soft center.
cards.depth: It matters again every time you paste a long document and tack 'and remember to do X' at the end. That lands in a strong position by luck; move it there on purpose. As contexts grow longer, the middle sag deepens, so the habit pays more the bigger your prompts get.

cards.hook: Short volatility pays you monthly, then bills you all at once.

cards.body: The variance risk premium is real, but its payoff is **negatively skewed**: a long run of small wins punctuated by rare, violent losses. Most months implied exceeds realized and you collect. Then one regime break hands back a year of premium in a week. This shape is why the Sharpe ratio flatters short-vol books. It rewards smooth upside and barely penalizes the fat left tail until the tail actually arrives. Sizing has to assume the loss month, not the median month.
cards.depth: The same skew defends the premium. If short vol paid smoothly, capital would flood in and compete it away. The pain of the tail is the barrier to entry, so the wage exists precisely because the ride is not smooth.

cards.hook: The first AI fair-use ruling went against the machine.
cards.body: In February 2025, Judge Bibas granted summary judgment to **Thomson Reuters** against Ross Intelligence, holding that copying Westlaw headnotes to train a legal-research tool was not fair use. Two things made it bite. The AI was non-generative, so it competed directly with the source instead of transforming it. And factor four, market harm, cut hard: Ross built a market substitute for Westlaw. Practitioners over-read it as a template for the generative cases. Bibas expressly noted his reasoning may not carry to systems that output new expression.
cards.depth: The same judge had denied summary judgment in 2023 and set the case for trial, then reversed himself on reconsideration. That reversal is the tell. Courts are still finding their footing, and an early ruling is a data point, not settled doctrine.

cards.hook: Your 90% confidence ranges are right about half the time.
cards.body: Ask people for a range they are 90% sure contains the answer, and the true value falls inside only **roughly 40 to 60%** of the time. The interval comes out too narrow because its width itself signals ignorance, and admitting ignorance feels like weakness. The fix is mechanical, not motivational: widen every interval until it feels slightly embarrassing, then widen once more. Calibration is a trainable skill, and the cheapest edge in any forecast is refusing to be as sure as you feel.
cards.depth: This is why point estimates lie. "It'll cost 40k" hides the range. Forcing an explicit low and high, then stretching both, surfaces the tail you were pretending away, and the tail is usually where the decision actually lives.

cards.hook: Pre-decide the trigger, not just the task.
cards.body: A to-do names what to do but leaves the hardest part, when and where, to a moment when your executive function is already taxed. **Implementation intentions** close that gap: you write "if situation X, then I do Y." When the trigger arrives, the action fires with far less deliberation, because you offloaded the decision to a rule instead of your working memory. Reported effect sizes across dozens of studies run medium to large. It works best for exactly the tasks you keep meaning to start and never do.
cards.depth: "When I sit down with coffee, I open the deal doc first" beats "review the deal doc." The cue does the initiating your brain won't. Attach the new action to something you already do reliably, and the existing habit becomes the trigger.

cards.hook: A week back, how many items does working memory really hold?
cards.body: The famous number is seven, from Miller's 1956 paper. The **better answer is about four**, per Cowan's later work, and often fewer once the items are unfamiliar or you are tired. This is not trivia for you. It is the whole case for externalizing: a checklist, a scratchpad, one visible next step. If the plan lives only in your head, you are asking a four-slot buffer to hold six things, and it will silently drop two. Put it on paper and the buffer is free to actually think.
cards.depth: Chunking is the loophole. Four chunks of familiar material can each carry a lot, which is why expertise feels like extra memory. It isn't more slots, it's richer contents in each one.

cards.hook: Rolling a loser for a credit is a new, bigger bet.
cards.body: When your short option goes against you, the popular move is to roll it out in time for a net credit, and it feels like you fixed the trade. You did not. You closed one position at a loss and opened a larger, longer-dated one, and the credit only exists because you added duration, size, or moved the strike closer to the money. The market did not hand you money; you sold more risk. **A roll is not repair, it is re-entry at worse odds.** If you would not open that new position fresh today, do not roll into it.
cards.depth: The credit is an accounting artifact: extrinsic value from the added time, minus the intrinsic you just absorbed. Traders anchor on 'never realize a loss,' so they chain rolls until one gap move on an oversized position ends the sequence. The discipline is to price the roll as a standalone trade, blind to the entry you are anchored to.

cards.hook: Using a dead actor's digital replica now needs estate consent.
cards.body: For years California's postmortem right of publicity (Civil Code 3344.1) covered a deceased personality's name, image, and likeness for 70 years, but it predated convincing synthetic performances. AB 1836, operative January 1, 2025, closes that gap: producing an audiovisual work with a digital replica of a deceased performer now requires consent from the estate. **The statute targets the replica specifically, not just the underlying likeness.** So a studio that licensed old footage does not automatically hold the right to generate new AI performances from it. Old grants may not reach synthetic resurrection.
cards.depth: The practitioner trap is treating a footage license or an old NIL grant as blanket authority. AB 1836 wants consent that references the digital replica's use with specificity, and it carves exceptions for news, satire, and documentary. For estates it is a new revenue line; for producers, a new clearance step before any generative resurrection.

cards.hook: Time-based reminders fail you. Event-based ones fire on their own.
cards.body: Prospective memory, remembering to do a thing later, comes in two flavors. Time-based ('call the pharmacy at 3') makes you monitor the clock yourself, which is exactly the self-cueing an ADHD brain does poorly. Event-based ('call the pharmacy when I get in the car') rides a cue the environment delivers for free. The fix is not a better alarm; it is to **anchor the new action to an event that already reliably happens.** After I pour coffee, I take the meds. The trigger stops depending on you noticing time, and starts depending on a thing the world does anyway.
cards.depth: This is Gollwitzer's implementation-intentions research, the 'when-then' plan. It helps everyone but disproportionately those with weak self-directed cueing. Stack the new behavior onto an existing anchor tied to a fixed action or place, never a time. The anchor carries the memory load your prefrontal cortex keeps dropping.

cards.hook: Your signal uses today's close. So does your fill. Impossible.
cards.body: A classic silent look-ahead: your rule says 'buy when today's close is above the 50-day average,' and your backtest fills the buy at today's close. But you cannot know the close until the session ends, and by then you can no longer trade at it. The signal and the execution share a price that exists only after trading stops. **The fix is a one-bar lag: signal on today's close, fill at tomorrow's open.** That single shift often erases most of a strategy's apparent edge, because the edge was living in a fill nobody could actually get.
cards.depth: This is distinct from slippage; the price is not merely optimistic, it is unobtainable in principle. The tell is a strategy whose returns collapse the moment you lag execution by one bar. Any signal built from a bar's own close, high, or low must execute on a later bar, or the backtest is quietly trading with tomorrow's newspaper.

cards.hook: Which is likelier: a bank teller, or a feminist bank teller?
cards.body: Take a beat before you answer. The vivid version, the feminist bank teller, feels more likely because it fits the story you were told about her. But every feminist bank teller is already a bank teller, so that group can only be smaller. **Adding a specific detail can never raise a probability, only lower it.** This is the conjunction fallacy: representativeness, how well a scenario matches a stereotype, hijacks your sense of likelihood. The richer and more convincing the picture, the fewer people it actually describes.
cards.depth: Why it bites you again: every detailed forecast, deal scenario, or risk narrative you find persuasive is paying a probability tax for its specificity. 'The market falls because of X, then Y, then Z' feels rigorous and is strictly less likely than 'the market falls.' Strip the conjunctions before you bet on the story.

cards.hook: Short an option, and hedging forces you to buy high, sell low.
cards.body: When you sell an option and delta-hedge, you are short gamma, so your delta moves against the tape. As price rises your position gets shorter and you must buy to stay neutral; as price falls you get longer and must sell. Every rehedge is buy-high, sell-low. That realized whipsaw is exactly the cost the premium pays you to bear. **You keep theta only if realized movement stays below the volatility you sold.** A quiet tape hands you the premium; a jumpy one bleeds it back one hedge at a time.
cards.depth: The whipsaw cost scales with gamma times the square of each move, which is why short-gamma books sit calm for weeks and then lose badly in a single gap. The danger was never the average day. It is the day the hedge cannot keep up.

cards.hook: Ask what happened to similar projects, not why yours is special.
cards.body: Facing a forecast, the instinct is to build it bottom-up from the specifics of your case. That inside view is where the planning fallacy lives: the details feel predictive, but mostly they manufacture optimism. The **outside view** starts elsewhere. Find the reference class of comparable efforts and take their base rate as your anchor. A remodel, a lawsuit, a product launch: the distribution of how those actually ended predicts your outcome better than your storyline does. Adjust from the base rate when hard evidence justifies it. Do not throw it away because your case feels unique.
cards.depth: Your project is one draw from a class, not a singular event. The uniqueness you feel is real but rarely bends the timeline much. Start at the class average, then move only as far as specific, verifiable evidence earns, not as far as your narrative wants.

cards.hook: Stop using your weakest system as your to-do list.
cards.body: Working memory is the exact function ADHD taxes hardest, and it is also what you lean on whenever you keep a plan in your head. Holding the next three steps active burns the same buffer you need to execute the current one, so the held items crowd out the doing. The move: **offload every open loop to one external surface the instant it appears.** Not five apps, one. A thought captured stops competing for the buffer. The aim is not tidiness; it is freeing the scarce resource so it can run the task actually in front of you.
cards.depth: This is why 'I'll remember to' fails specifically for you. The intention itself occupies the buffer until it either fires or evaporates, and under load it evaporates. Externalizing converts a memory task, which you are bad at, into a looking task, which you are not.

cards.hook: A blanket 'AI replica' grant can be void in California.
cards.body: California's AB 2602, in force since 2025, makes a contract term letting a producer create and use a **digital replica** of a performer's voice or likeness unenforceable in one specific situation: the term lacks a reasonably specific description of the intended uses, and the performer had neither legal counsel nor a union representative negotiating it. The prong practitioners miss is specificity. A sweeping 'any and all AI uses in perpetuity' grant does not get safer with more boilerplate. **Vagueness is the defect the statute punishes.** Describe the uses concretely, or watch the grant collapse.
cards.depth: It pairs with AB 1836, which requires estate consent for replicas of deceased performers. Together they mark California's direction of travel: consent to synthesize a person is only as strong as its specificity and its process, never as strong as the breadth of language you manage to draft.

cards.hook: You can win a trade and still have it cancelled.
cards.body: In March 2022, nickel on the London Metal Exchange rocketed past $100,000 a tonne in hours, a short squeeze cascading through a giant producer's hedge. Traders on the right side were suddenly, enormously in the money. Then the LME did something rare: it **halted the market and cancelled the day's trades**, rewinding prices to the prior close. Winners' gains vanished by fiat. Underneath the chaos sits the lesson: your profit is a claim against a venue and its rulebook, not a law of nature. Exchange discretion is a risk that never shows up in a backtest.
cards.depth: Tsingshan, the short, dodged a catastrophic loss; the funds who were right sued and mostly lost in UK courts. It rhymes with past futures blowups on the theme of financing, but adds a newer twist: governance risk. The counterparty of last resort can change the rules while you still hold the position.

cards.hook: Put skew is a hedging tax, not a crash forecast.
cards.body: Index put skew - the premium of downside implied vol over upside - is far steeper than the actual asymmetry of returns justifies. The driver isn't a better crash forecast. It's **structural demand for downside insurance**: pensions, funds with drawdown mandates, and overwriters all lean the same way, bidding puts and pressing calls. That persistent imbalance is a risk premium, harvestable through risk reversals or put ratios. The catch is what you inherit. Selling skew leaves you short the exact tail everyone else is paying to avoid, so the premium is rent for standing under the thing that falls.
cards.depth: Equity index skew steepened structurally after 1987, when the crash taught dealers that downside gaps are real and put demand became permanent. Pre-1987 index options showed little skew at all. The premium you collect selling it is compensation for absorbing that lesson on everyone else's behalf.

cards.hook: Denmark wants to give you copyright in your own face.
cards.body: In mid-2025 Denmark's government proposed something no copyright regime has done: granting each citizen an intellectual-property right in their own **face, body, and voice**. The theory reframes deepfakes as infringement rather than defamation or privacy harm, so a person could demand takedown of a synthetic likeness the way a studio pulls a pirated film. It reportedly covers realistic digital imitations and carves out parody and satire. The mechanism matters because IP rights transfer, license, and survive. A privacy claim dies with you, but a copyright-style likeness right could be assigned, inherited, and enforced platform-side.
cards.depth: Contrast the US patchwork: right of publicity is state law, varies wildly, and in most states is a commercial-appropriation tort, not property a platform must proactively honor. A copyright-style frame flips the default from opt-out enforcement to opt-in licensing, and hands the takedown machinery of copyright to individuals.

cards.hook: The hot hand was real. The famous study had a bug.
cards.body: For thirty years the hot hand in basketball was the textbook case of humans seeing patterns in randomness. Then in 2018 Miller and Sanjurjo found a subtle flaw in the original analysis. If you take a finite sequence of coin flips and measure how often a head follows a head, the answer is **below 50 percent, not equal to it** - a selection effect baked into how streaks get counted. Correcting for it, the original data actually showed a real hot-hand effect. The lesson isn't about basketball. It's that a bias correction you never thought to check can flip a conclusion outright.
cards.depth: The bias: conditioning on 'the previous flip was heads' shortens the pool of eligible next-flips in a way that favors tails. In a length-100 sequence the expected conditional rate runs a few points under half. Small sample, invisible skew, thirty years of confident citation.

cards.hook: A reward next month barely exists to your brain today.
cards.body: Delay discounting is the rate at which a future reward loses value as it moves further away. Everyone discounts; the ADHD curve just drops **steeper and faster**, so a payoff two weeks out carries almost no motivational pull in the present. This is why 'it matters for my career' fails to start a task while 'it's due in an hour' works instantly - the deadline drags the reward into the now. The move isn't more willpower. It's engineering the payoff closer: stake money you lose today, tell someone you'll report back tonight, or split the goal so a real win lands within the hour.
cards.depth: Same mechanism sits under why body-doubling and deadlines work. They don't add discipline, they compress the distance to a consequence. Anything that converts a distant abstract reward into a near concrete one is working the curve instead of fighting it.

cards.hook: Why isn't fifteen years of daily returns fifteen years of evidence?
cards.body: You've got thousands of daily observations and a clean equity curve. Statistics only pay you for one thing, though, and it isn't row count. Give it a beat before you read on. The answer: **independence**. Daily returns clump into regimes - one bull, one crash, one recovery - so a model fit across 2010 to 2021 mostly saw a single macro environment wearing thousands of costumes. Its effective sample might be two or three. That's why strategies 'validated on fifteen years' die in year sixteen: they were tuned against a handful of regimes and read the calendar as the sample.
cards.depth: Same trap hides in cross-validation on time series: shuffle the days and adjacent-regime leakage inflates every score. The honest count is regimes survived, not observations logged - which is why walk-forward across distinct environments tells you more than another decade inside the same one.

cards.hook: Your covered call is a short put in disguise.
cards.body: Put-call parity forces it. Long stock plus a short call equals a short put plus a bond, so a **covered call and a cash-secured put** at the same strike and expiry carry the same payoff shape, the same max profit, and the same downside. The 'conservative income' label on covered calls and the 'risky' label on naked puts describe one identical risk. If you would not sell the put, you have no business writing the call. The only real differences are financing, dividends, and early-assignment path, not the exposure you are actually taking on.
cards.depth: Parity says C minus P equals S minus the discounted strike. Rearranged, long-stock-short-call equals a short put plus lending the strike. The bond piece is a constant vertical shift, so it moves the breakeven but not the shape. Assignment timing and dividend capture differ, which is why the two are not literally interchangeable in a taxable, dividend-paying account.

cards.hook: The MFN you grant is a free option on your future deals.
cards.body: A most-favored-nations clause promises party A your best terms. Its real cost is not felt today. It is that every future negotiation now carries a hidden liability: any concession you make to party B ratchets back to A automatically. You have **written a free option** on your own future flexibility, and the counterparty holds it at zero premium. Seasoned drafters price this by narrowing scope hard: same category of licensee, same territory, same term length, economic terms only. The unscoped MFN across all future deals is the one that quietly detonates years later.
cards.depth: Scope levers that actually contain it: comparability baskets, so only genuinely like deals trigger the clause; economic-only, excluding creative or approval rights; a sunset date; and a carve-out for affiliate or bundled transactions. The broadest version, all terms and all future deals, silently turns every later negotiation into a three-party negotiation you never invited the first party to attend.

cards.hook: In 2006, one fund lost $6.6 billion on a gas spread.
cards.body: Amaranth Advisors bet on natural gas calendar spreads through trader Brian Hunter. The thesis itself was not crazy. The problem was scale: the fund's positions were a reported outsized fraction of open interest in the contracts it traded, so Amaranth was no longer betting on the market, it had **become the market**. When the spread turned against it in September 2006, there was no one to sell to at a sane price, and every attempt to exit pushed the spread further away. Roughly $6.6 billion evaporated in about a week. The lesson is not that spreads are dangerous. It is that size relative to liquidity is its own greek.
cards.depth: Liquidity risk is invisible in a backtest that assumes you trade at the mid. It surfaces only when your own exit is the largest order in the book. The tell is simple: if unwinding your position would move the price against you, you do not really hold a position of that size, you hold a claim you cannot actually sell. Size to the exit, not the entry.

cards.hook: Toddlers barely learn from a screen a live person would teach them.
cards.body: Show a toddler under about two and a half a task on video, and show another child the identical task performed live, and the live group learns it markedly better. Researchers call the gap the **video deficit**. Same content, same demonstrator, but the screen version underperforms until roughly age three. The likely mechanism is that very young brains treat flat, non-responsive video as not-quite-real, and learning at that age is tuned to live social interaction. The practical read: 'educational' video for a one-year-old is mostly entertainment, whatever the box promises.
cards.depth: The rescue is contingency, not resolution. In studies, real-time video chat where the adult responds live produces close to in-person learning, while the same adult pre-recorded does not. So for the under-three set the useful frame is not screen-versus-no-screen, it is responsive-versus-broadcast. A video call with a person answering back teaches. A polished cartoon covering the same word largely does not, yet.

cards.hook: Models read the start and end of your prompt. The middle blurs.
cards.body: Give a model a long context and ask it to use a fact buried inside, and accuracy depends heavily on where that fact sits. Performance is highest when the needed information is at the very beginning or the very end, and it sags in the middle. Researchers named the effect **'lost in the middle.'** The attention pattern is roughly U-shaped, not uniform, so a critical instruction dropped into the center of a long context can be quietly underweighted even though it is technically present and retrievable. The build implication: put the task and the load-bearing constraints at the top or the bottom, never in the soft middle.
cards.depth: Two practical moves. First, restate the actual task at the end of a long prompt, after the reference material, so it lands in the high-attention zone. Second, do not pad: adding marginally relevant context can shove the important part into the weak middle and lower accuracy, so retrieval that returns fewer, better chunks often beats returning more. Position is a lever you control for free.

cards.hook: Implied vol beats realized most months. That spread is the wage.
cards.body: Over long samples of index options, option-implied volatility sits a few points above the volatility that later shows up in the underlying. Sellers of that insurance collect the difference, the **variance risk premium**, and it is one of the most persistent edges in markets. But it is not a mispricing to arbitrage away. It is payment for holding a position that loses badly in crashes, exactly when your other assets fall too. The premium is the fee for absorbing that correlated tail. It pays steadily, then hands some back all at once.
cards.depth: The premium concentrates in downside strikes, which is why put skew is steep and why naive 'sell the wings' books look brilliant right up until a Volmageddon. The honest read: this is risk transfer, not alpha. Size it like insurance underwriting, where one bad year can erase several good ones, and the edge only compounds if you survive the payout.

cards.hook: Praise seems to hurt performance, criticism seems to help. Both illusions.
cards.body: Israeli flight instructors told Kahneman that praising a cadet after a great maneuver was followed by a worse one, while chewing out a bad maneuver was followed by improvement. So praise hurt and punishment worked. Both conclusions were **regression to the mean** wearing a causal mask. Exceptional results are part skill, part luck, and the luck does not repeat, so the next attempt drifts back toward average no matter what you said. Intervene right after any extreme outcome and the expected bounce-back will flatter or frame whatever you did.
cards.depth: This quietly corrupts trading journals and management alike. Cut a strategy after its worst month and it 'recovers' once you are out. Reward a trader after a hot streak and they cool. The fix is a control: compare against the base rate of what follows extremes anyway, not against your memory of what you changed. Mean reversion is the null hypothesis your intervention has to beat.

cards.hook: A second person in the room does your regulating for you.
cards.body: Body doubling means working next to someone, in person or on a video call, while you each do your own separate task. It works because ADHD is a deficit of **self-directed regulation**, not of ability, and another person's presence supplies from outside the structure your prefrontal system supplies unreliably from inside. Their attention raises the task's salience and adds a thin thread of accountability, so starting and staying both cost less. Nothing is delegated and no one touches your work. You are borrowing an external regulator to run an internal function.
cards.depth: This is why the same task is impossible alone and easy in a cafe or on a coworking call. Choose a partner you would rather not look idle in front of, and keep the task visible between you. The mechanism is identical to the one behind deadlines and public commitments: outsource the executive function you cannot summon on command.

cards.hook: Your fully AI-generated ad may belong to no one, including you.
cards.body: US copyright protects works of human authorship, and courts have held that output generated autonomously by a machine has no author to protect. The D.C. Circuit and the Copyright Office have both landed there: an image a model produces from your prompt is, standing alone, **uncopyrightable**. Prompts are treated as instructions, not authorship, because you do not control the output the way an author controls a sentence. The trap is assuming that elaborate prompting earns you a copyright. It does not. What you can protect is the human selection, arrangement, and editing you layer on top.
cards.depth: This inverts the usual worry. The risk is not only that a model copied someone else. It is that your own generated asset falls straight into the public domain, where a competitor can lawfully lift it. Register what a human meaningfully authored, document that contribution, and treat raw model output as unowned until a person shapes it into something.

cards.hook: Two words turn adjacent scenes into a story. Which two?
cards.body: You already met this one, from Trey Parker and Matt Stone. Read your outline and listen to the word joining each beat to the next. One connector is fatal; two are alive. Take a second before the reveal. The fatal link is 'and then,' which only sets events side by side. The living ones are **'but' and 'therefore.'** Reversal and consequence, the two shapes of causation that make an audience lean forward. If the only honest word between two scenes is 'and then,' they are adjacent, not connected, and the engine is off.
cards.depth: It bites hardest in the audio fiction you produce, where a listener has no picture to coast on and drifts the instant causation drops. Run the connective test on every episode outline before you record, and where a stretch only earns 'and then,' collapse it or find the 'but' that turns it. Recalling the rule cold, not just recognizing it, is what makes it fire while you are actually drafting.

cards.hook: Pinned at your strike, assignment is a coin flip.
cards.body: An option that expires a penny in the money is almost always exercised. One that finishes exactly at the strike is not. Holders decide based on their own book, after-hours moves, and rounding, so some exercise and some don't. That leaves you, the short, guessing. You close Friday believing you're flat, then learn over the weekend you were assigned, now unexpectedly long or short stock into Monday's gap. **The danger isn't the option, it's the position you didn't know you inherited.** Close or roll tight at-the-money shorts before the bell rather than betting on the coin flip.
cards.depth: The OCC auto-exercises anything at least a penny in the money, but the holder can file a contrary instruction until the deadline, and true at-the-money sits right on that knife edge. Cash-settled index options avoid share assignment entirely, which is one reason many premium sellers prefer them for expiration-week positions.

cards.hook: A judge handed AI plaintiffs the winning theory they ignored.
cards.body: In June 2025, a federal judge ruled Meta's training of its Llama models on copyrighted books was fair use, and the authors lost. But he said they lost because they argued the wrong case, not because Meta was right. The theory he flagged as the live one is **market dilution**: not that the model copied your book, but that it can now flood the market with competing works and gut demand for the originals. Most practitioners are still fighting over the input, whether their text sat in the training set. The judge signaled the next war is on the output.
cards.depth: The same week, a different San Francisco judge reached the opposite emphasis in the Anthropic case, calling the training 'exceedingly transformative.' Two judges, two roadmaps: one for defendants on transformation, one for plaintiffs on market harm. Fair use is a four-factor balance, and 2025 showed the fourth factor, effect on the market, is where these cases will actually be decided.

cards.hook: The fills your backtest assumes are the ones you'd miss.
cards.body: A backtest fills your order at the closing or mid price. Live, a resting limit order only executes when someone crosses it, which happens precisely when the market is moving through your price against you. So the trades you actually get filled on are adversely selected: you buy right before it keeps falling, you sell right before it keeps rising. **Mean-reversion strategies are flattered worst**, because the clean reversion trades are exactly the ones where nobody would have hit your resting order. The backtest booked profits on fills that, in the real book, never would have happened.
cards.depth: One partial check: re-run assuming you cross to the far touch and pay the spread, and add a fill probability below one for passive orders. If the edge evaporates, it was living inside the fill assumption, not the signal. Marketable orders dodge the selection bias but pay the spread every time, which is its own drag. Either way, the mid-price fill is a fiction.

cards.hook: ADHD's core deficit isn't attention. It's the missing pause.
cards.body: Barkley's model reframes the whole disorder: the primary deficit is response inhibition, the split-second pause between a stimulus and your reaction to it. Attention, working memory, and emotional control all sit downstream of that pause, because the pause is what buys the time to deploy them. Miss it, and you've acted before the executive machinery could load. The practical consequence: **you can't reliably manufacture the pause from the inside, so build it on the outside.** Put physical friction between you and the distractor. Log out, move the phone to another room. You're not adding willpower. You're rebuilding the gap the brain skips.
cards.depth: This is also why 'just focus' fails as advice: focus is a downstream product, not the lever. The lever is the environment around the pause. It reframes distraction too. The distractor isn't beating your attention, it's beating your inhibition, arriving before you could decline it. Change what can reach you in that first unguarded instant.

cards.hook: In 2018, short-vol funds hedged themselves off a cliff.
cards.body: February 5, 2018. Volatility had been dead for a year, and a crowd of inverse-VIX products, the largest called XIV, paid you to bet it stayed dead. Each had to rebalance daily by buying VIX futures whenever volatility rose. That afternoon it rose, so they bought, which pushed the futures higher, which forced them to buy more. The loop ran until XIV lost roughly 96% in hours and was shut down. **When a crowded trade's required hedging feeds the very thing it's exposed to, it becomes its own accelerant.** The move didn't kill them. Their reaction to it did.
cards.depth: The rebalance buying was concentrated in the last hour, which is why the worst of it landed near the close. The lesson rhymes with LTCM and the 2010 flash crash: leverage plus mechanical, price-triggered flows turns a normal move into a discontinuous one. Liquidity is thinnest exactly when everyone's rules demand the same trade at the same second.

cards.hook: A dividend is the only reason to exercise a call early.
cards.body: Textbooks say never exercise an American call early, because you throw away the remaining time value. The exception is the day before a stock goes ex-dividend. Holding the call, you do not collect the dividend; exercising converts it to stock in time to capture the payout. It is only worth it when the dividend exceeds the call's remaining extrinsic value, which happens on deep in-the-money calls with little time value left. **Miss that window and your short call gets assigned when you least expect it.** The assignment is not random. It is a rational dividend grab.
cards.depth: This is why brokers flag early-assignment risk around ex-dividend dates on short in-the-money calls. If you are short a call carrying less extrinsic value than the upcoming dividend, assume you will be assigned. The defensive move is to close or roll before the ex-dividend date, not gamble on the counterparty's inattention.

cards.hook: The 2023 guild deal splits digital replicas into two kinds.
cards.body: The 2023 SAG-AFTRA contract does not treat all AI likenesses the same. An **employment-based digital replica** is built from work the performer actually did on that production; an independently created digital replica is one the studio makes from other sources or from scratch. The distinction drives the money. For the employment-based kind, the performer must consent and generally be paid for the days the replica is used, as if they had worked them. Practitioners who lump both together miss that consent and compensation hinge on how the replica was created, not just on whether it resembles the actor.
cards.depth: The taxonomy matters for drafting. A blanket 'digital replica' consent clause can be under-inclusive or overreaching, because the guild floor attaches different rights to each category, plus a separate bucket for fully synthetic performers with no underlying human. Get it wrong and you either shortchange a payment or claim a consent the performer never actually gave.

cards.hook: Adding a detail can only lower a probability, never raise it.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><ellipse cx="180" cy="118" rx="150" ry="92" fill="none" stroke="#d9a441" stroke-width="2"/><text x="180" y="44" fill="#a89f8d" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="15" text-anchor="middle">bank tellers</text><ellipse cx="160" cy="138" rx="70" ry="48" fill="none" stroke="#7fb4a2" stroke-width="2"/><text x="160" y="135" fill="#a89f8d" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle">feminist</text><text x="160" y="151" fill="#a89f8d" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle">bank tellers</text><text x="200" y="228" fill="#a89f8d" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle">the subset can't be likelier than the whole</text></svg>
cards.body: Kahneman and Tversky described Linda: a philosophy major, outspoken on social justice. Asked which is more likely, that she is a bank teller, or a bank teller and a feminist, most people pick the second. It cannot be. Feminist bank tellers sit inside the set of bank tellers, so that group is **always at least as improbable as the larger category alone**. Detail makes a story feel representative, and representativeness gets mistaken for probability. The more vivid and specific a scenario, the more plausible it feels and the less likely it actually is.
cards.depth: The trap shows up wherever you build a case. A detailed trial narrative, a market thesis with five confirming reasons, a granular forecast: each added clause feels like evidence but multiplies the ways the whole can be wrong. Strip a prediction to its load-bearing claim and score that, not the story wrapped around it.

cards.hook: How many items does working memory really hold? Not seven.
cards.body: You saw that Miller's famous 'seven plus or minus two' is mostly a myth for raw capacity. Take a beat before the number lands. Once researchers like Nelson Cowan stripped out the rehearsal and chunking that inflate the count, the honest limit came in near **four chunks**. So the checklist you are about to hand someone, the interface you are designing, the spoken instruction to your kid: if it asks them to juggle more than about four fresh things at once, it exceeds the hardware. Chunk it, or put the overflow on paper.
cards.depth: Retrieval is the point of this card, not the fact. Every time you pull 'four, not seven' back out of memory instead of rereading it, you deepen the trace. The applied version is a rule you will use this week: assume four, and anything past four needs external scaffolding, whether a written list, a template, or a visible countdown.

cards.hook: The marshmallow test mostly measured the household, not willpower.
cards.body: The 1970s Stanford studies claimed a preschooler who waited for a second treat did better in life decades later. A 2018 replication with a far larger, more representative sample told a quieter story. Once researchers controlled for family income and home environment, **much of the predictive power faded**. Waiting was largely a proxy for a stable, resourced household, where a child has good reason to trust that a promised reward will actually arrive. The lesson is not to drill your toddler on delay. It is that trust and stability teach patience better than a stopwatch.
cards.depth: There is a deeper mechanism worth keeping. Delay of gratification is not a fixed trait a child either has or lacks; it is partly a rational read of the environment. Kids who have learned that promises get broken grab the sure thing, correctly. Change the reliability of the world around them and their patience changes with it.

cards.hook: An at-the-money call's delta is above 0.50, not at it.
cards.body: Struck at the forward, a call's d1 term equals half sigma-root-T, which is positive. So its delta, N(d1), sits just above 0.50, and it climbs with more time or higher vol. The reason is structural: a lognormal price has its median below its mean, so the strike that gives a true coin-flip finish lies slightly out of the money relative to the forward. **A 'symmetric' at-the-money straddle is quietly long delta.** Retail treats 50-delta as the ATM anchor, but the forward, not spot, is the real center of mass.
cards.depth: How much? At 20% vol and one month, half-sigma-root-T is about 0.03, nudging delta to roughly 0.51. Stretch to a year and it is near 0.54. Small, yes. But your 'delta-neutral' short straddle then needs a few shares of hedge you probably never put on.

cards.hook: The Warhol ruling quietly reloaded every AI fair-use defense.
cards.body: In 2023 the Supreme Court, in Warhol v Goldsmith, narrowed transformative use: a new meaning or message no longer saves a copy if the use serves the **same commercial purpose** as the original. AI training defenses had leaned hard on transformativeness. Now a plaintiff can argue that a model trained on their work to make competing work shares that work's purpose, weakening factor one before factor four is even reached. Practitioners still cite pre-Warhol wins like Google v Oracle as if the ground has not shifted. It has.
cards.depth: The nuance the headlines missed: Warhol touched only factor one, and the Court called it a narrow holding. But 'same purpose' is exactly the wedge in AI suits, since a model that outputs marketable images arguably competes with the images it trained on. Whether courts stretch it from one Prince photo to a billion-image corpus is the open question.

cards.hook: Your reminder system stops working the day it stops being new.
cards.body: The mechanism is salience. An ADHD brain allocates attention by how much a cue stands out, not by how much it matters. A new checklist, a fresh sticky note, a just-built app all grab you because novelty spikes the signal. Two weeks later the cue is furniture and your eye slides past it. This is **tool decay**, and it is why every system you build works for a while and then quietly dies. The fix is not a better system. It is changing the cue's form on a schedule: move it, recolor it, reword it, so novelty keeps the signal alive.
cards.depth: Practical version: stop chasing the perfect permanent system, because it will decay no matter how good it is. Build one that is cheap to refresh instead. A whiteboard you rewrite every Sunday beats an elegant app you stop seeing by Wednesday. The refresh is the feature, not a sign the tool failed.

cards.hook: Fifteen years of daily data is not 3,750 independent tests.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><text x="200" y="26" fill="#a89f8d" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="15" text-anchor="middle">Two ways to size the same 11 years</text><line x1="40" y1="70" x2="360" y2="70" stroke="#7fb4a2" stroke-width="10"/><text x="200" y="98" fill="#7fb4a2" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle">3,750 daily rows</text><rect x="40" y="140" width="120" height="40" fill="none" stroke="#d9a441" stroke-width="2"/><rect x="170" y="140" width="70" height="40" fill="none" stroke="#d9a441" stroke-width="2"/><rect x="250" y="140" width="110" height="40" fill="none" stroke="#d9a441" stroke-width="2"/><text x="100" y="165" fill="#a89f8d" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle">bull</text><text x="205" y="165" fill="#a89f8d" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle">crash</text><text x="305" y="165" fill="#a89f8d" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle">recovery</text><text x="200" y="206" fill="#d9a441" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle">3 independent regimes</text><text x="200" y="230" fill="#a89f8d" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle">your t-stat trusts the top row</text></svg>
cards.body: A backtest brags about sample size in observations, but statistics only reward **independent** observations. Daily returns clump into regimes: a low-vol bull, a crash, a recovery. A strategy fit on 2010 to 2021 mostly saw one macro environment, falling rates and rising multiples, dressed up as thousands of data points. Its real out-of-sample count might be two or three. That is why models 'validated on 15 years' die in year sixteen. They were tuned against a handful of regimes while reading the calendar as if it were the sample.
cards.depth: The discipline: count regimes, not rows. Ask how many genuinely different environments the data spans, rate cycles, vol regimes, liquidity states, and treat that as your degrees of freedom. A Sharpe earned across four regimes outranks one earned across four thousand correlated days inside a single regime.

cards.hook: You met the seven-year rule. What made it bite?
cards.body: The cap comes from **California Labor Code section 2855**, which holds any personal-service contract to seven years. Studios used to gut it by tolling the clock every time an actor refused a role and drew a suspension, stretching a seven-year deal across a decade. In 1944 Olivia de Havilland won the reading that seven years means seven calendar years of the contract's life, not seven years of service actually rendered. That is the whole mechanism: suspensions stopped pausing the clock. It is why the statute still governs long artist and recording deals today.
cards.depth: Modern echo: recording artists have invoked 2855 to break out of multi-album deals, running the same calendar-years logic. Labels push back with claims for undelivered albums. The tension De Havilland pried open, service rendered versus term elapsed, has never fully closed.

cards.hook: Selling index options is mostly selling correlation.
cards.body: An index option's vol is built from two ingredients: component vols and the correlation binding them. Back out the correlation implied by index options versus single-name options and you find it **persistently trades above what correlation subsequently realizes**. That gap is why the index variance risk premium runs fatter than the average single-stock premium - the difference is a correlation risk premium. Dispersion desks harvest it directly: short index vol, long a basket of single-name vols, sized so aggregate vol exposure roughly cancels. What remains is a pure bet that stocks move together less than the market fears. Sell an index straddle and that is mostly what you are collecting.
cards.depth: The premium exists because correlation spikes exactly when it hurts. In a crash, pairwise correlations lurch toward one, index vol explodes relative to the basket, and short-correlation books take their worst mark. Like the vol risk premium itself, it is insurance income: paid for bearing a left tail that arrives on everyone's worst day. CBOE's implied correlation indexes let you watch the spread directly.

cards.hook: In London, Stable Diffusion's weights are not a copy.
cards.body: In November 2025 the UK High Court delivered the first major ruling on whether an AI model is itself an infringing copy of its training data. Getty had dropped its core training and output claims mid-trial, leaving secondary infringement: did Stability import an 'infringing copy' of Getty's images into the UK in the form of Stable Diffusion? No, held the court, because the weights **store and reproduce none of the training images**. The model is not a copy, even though copies were unquestionably used to make it. Getty salvaged a narrow trademark win over generated watermarks. The model-as-derivative-of-its-corpus theory just took its first direct hit on the merits.
cards.depth: The ruling blesses less than headlines suggest. Getty abandoned the training and output claims for jurisdictional and evidentiary reasons, so UK law on training itself remains open, and Getty's parallel US case against Stability continues in Delaware. But the weights holding travels: if a model is not a copy of its corpus, distributing the model is not distributing the works.

cards.hook: Two underwriters, same file, quotes 55 percent apart.
cards.body: When Kahneman's team asked an insurer's executives how far apart two underwriters would land pricing the same policy, the guesses centered near 10 percent. The audit's reported answer: a median gap of 55 percent. The mechanism is that **noise is invisible in the single case**. A biased shop at least leaves a pattern you can catch; noisy judgments each look reasonable alone, and the scatter only appears when two professionals judge the identical file, which almost no organization stages. In squared-error terms, noise degrades accuracy exactly as much as the same amount of bias. Any desk pricing deals or grading risk runs a lottery it has never audited.
cards.depth: System noise splits into level noise (some graders run harsh), pattern noise (idiosyncratic reactions to specific cases), and occasion noise (the same person on a different day). The cheap countermeasure is decision hygiene: collect independent judgments before anyone talks, then aggregate. Averaging independent reads cuts noise by the square root of the count - two readers buy roughly a 29 percent reduction.
